items.title: Game Mashups: Creative but Labor-Intensive
points: Gamers use AI agents to merge video games like Mario Kart and Call of Duty, taking 3-4 hours of iteration but requiring no coding knowledge.
Someone embedded 1,000+ Minecraft items into Elden Ring, including creepers that attack the game's hardest bosses.
Another creator integrated Mario Kart mechanics into Call of Duty's zombie mode, allowing players to run over zombies and throw bananas.
A GitHub guide estimates the merge process takes 3-4 hours for experienced users: tell an AI agent what you want, then iterate through broken features.
The real friction point is verbal precision (describing bugs exactly), not coding ability; rough first versions are typical without a guide or reference project.

items.title: Houdini's AI Resurrection and the Ethics of Authenticity
points: AI reconstructed Harry Houdini's face from 400+ historical photos for a new TV series, premiering October 14th for the 100-year anniversary of his death.
Real actors performed all movements and sequences, then AI swapped their faces using the archival photos and footage (face-swapping: digitally replacing one person's face with another's in video).
The three-episode series explores Houdini's rivalry with his brother and his decades spent debunking fake mediums, ironic given his own AI resurrection.

Producers were transparent about production methods with no intent to deceive, distinguishing this from AI-generated deepfakes (synthetic media that falsely depicts someone saying or doing something).

items.title: Local AI Eliminates Privacy Trade-offs
points: Raspberry Pi's AI HAT+ 2 is a dedicated chip that lets users run chatbots, translation, and object detection entirely on-device, with no data sent to remote servers.
Use cases include querying private documents, analyzing home security footage, and processing sensitive information while keeping full local control.
Trade-off: smaller on-device models have reduced capabilities compared to cloud-based AI, but privacy is preserved for users willing to accept the limits.

items.title: Nikon's AI Disqualification Sets Precedent for Science Contests
points: Nikon disqualified a Small World in Motion contest winner after discovering AI was used to enhance a microscope image of moving cell hairs.
Online scientists flagged the time-lapse as potentially AI-fabricated, prompting Nikon's investigation after judges had already selected it as the winner.
The winner claimed AI was used only to enhance clarity, not to generate imagery, but Nikon ruled this violated originality criteria.

The case highlights that detection lags behind submission, and that the line between legitimate image enhancement and generative alteration is increasingly hard to define, especially since scientists routinely process images before publication.

items.title: Fruit Fly Brain Uploaded to a Computer
points: Scientists sliced a fruit fly's brain into 7,000 pieces and used AI to reconstruct its neurons digitally.

The resulting digital copy moves and eats within a virtual body, marking what researchers call the closest real step toward mind uploading (transferring a brain's structure and function into a computer simulation).
